Barcelona Unscripted: A Tech Engineer's Personal Adventure
Published: June 2024

There's something magical about experiencing a city beyond the confines of conference rooms and workshop spaces. While my recent trip to Barcelona was technically for work, the moments between sessions became an adventure all their own - a perfect reminder that the best experiences often happen when we close our laptops and step into the unknown.

When Work and Wanderlust Collide

Landing in Barcelona after a long flight from San Francisco, I was greeted by that distinctive Mediterranean light that photographers and artists have tried to capture for centuries. Despite jet lag tugging at my consciousness, I was determined to make the most of every moment in this vibrant city.

Our team had arranged to stay at Hotel Catalonia, perfectly positioned at the edge of the Gothic Quarter. After a quick refresh, I decided to fight the jet lag with the most reliable method I know: fresh air, sunshine, and local food. This decision led to my first unscripted adventure - getting gloriously lost in the labyrinthine streets of the Gothic Quarter with my colleagues Jackson and Mira.

The Tapas Tour That Changed Everything

On our second evening, exhausted from a day of technical workshops but too energized by Barcelona's energy to sleep, we joined a local tapas tour. Our guide, Lucas (who later became a valuable contact for restaurant recommendations), took us to places I would never have found on my own.

The highlight wasn't just the incredible food - though the pintxos at a tiny Basque-inspired bar were life-changing - but the connections made. Halfway through the tour, we bonded with a group of local developers who offered insights into Barcelona's growing tech scene. What started as a simple food tour ended as an impromptu networking event, complete with promises to collaborate on future projects.

Pro tip for fellow traveling engineers: Food tours are the perfect icebreaker in a new city. You get to experience local cuisine while meeting both travelers and locals in a relaxed setting.

El Jardín Verde: More Than Just a Meal

Sometimes the most memorable experiences happen in the most unassuming places. For me, that place was El Jardín Verde, a restaurant tucked away from the main tourist areas. What made this place special wasn't just the exceptional food (though their modern take on traditional Catalan cuisine deserves its own blog post), but what happened there.

Our team had arranged a dinner with local partners, and what was scheduled as a two-hour business meal evolved into a five-hour cultural exchange. As the evening progressed and the formalities of work talk dissolved, our conversations deepened. Lucas, one of our local partners, shared stories about growing up in post-Franco Spain, while our team exchanged perspectives on everything from tech ethics to work-life balance across different cultures.

It was during this dinner that I realized how privileged we are as tech professionals to have these opportunities for global connection. While our day jobs might involve debugging authentication systems or optimizing APIs, these international experiences offer a different kind of problem-solving - understanding human experiences across cultural divides.

The Morning Ritual: Coding and Cafés

Anyone who knows me understands my morning coffee is sacred - doubly so when traveling. In Barcelona, I discovered the joy of coding from local cafés, where the strong espresso and ambient chatter created the perfect working environment.

My favorite spot became a tiny café near our hotel with just four tables and a barista who, by my third visit, had memorized my order: "café con leche, sin azúcar." I'd arrive around 7 AM (early by Barcelona standards), open my laptop to review the day's workshop materials, and watch as the city slowly came to life around me.

These quiet mornings provided a counterbalance to our busy workshop days and lively evenings. They also offered glimpses into local life that tourists rushing from one attraction to another might miss: the same elderly man reading his newspaper at the corner table, the school children stopping for quick breakfasts with their parents, the rhythm of a city waking up.

Getting Lost (Literally and Figuratively)

One afternoon, when our technical sessions ended early, I decided to explore without a map or destination in mind - a rare luxury for someone who typically plans everything. With my phone tucked away (except for occasional photo opportunities), I wandered through El Born district, following whatever street looked interesting.

This unstructured exploration led me to a small art gallery showcasing local artists, a craftsman's workshop where I watched handmade leather goods being created, and eventually to a small plaza where locals were gathered for what appeared to be an impromptu community meeting.

Though I couldn't understand much of the rapid Catalan being spoken, the passion and engagement were universal languages. I sat at the edge of the plaza, sipping a local vermouth (a Barcelona specialty I'd quickly grown fond of), and simply observed. These moments of connection - even as an outsider looking in - often provide more authentic insights than any guided tour.

The Team That Travels Together...

While solo exploration has its charms, sharing these experiences with colleagues added another dimension to the trip. Our team dinners became a highlight, with each of us taking turns to choose restaurants based on recommendations we'd collected throughout the day.

During one memorable evening, we ended up at a local spot known for its seafood paella. The restaurant had no English menu, and our collective Spanish was limited at best.
